name: Enamel reshaping / contouring

lead: Enamel reshaping smooths chips, evens out edges and slightly changes the length or shape of a tooth, mostly on the front teeth. People use it for quick, subtle fixes to teeth that are almost right already.

A dentist removes a thin layer of enamel using fine diamond burs, discs, strips or lasers, then polishes the surface. The change is visible straight away. It is described as a subtle change rather than a fix for major alignment problems, and no clinical studies specific to the procedure were found.

paras: It is usually a single-visit treatment, and since enamel has no nerve endings it often needs no anaesthetic. People often pair it with whitening or bonding, and it is a common small step in a smile makeover.
Enamel does not grow back, so the change is permanent. Taking off too much can expose dentin and cause temporary sensitivity.

angle.text: Enamel reshaping is used for quick, subtle fixes to uneven edges, chips and slightly long or pointed teeth, mostly on front teeth. A dentist shaves a thin layer of enamel and polishes it, and the change is visible straight away.

lead: Enamel reshaping, also called enamel contouring, enameloplasty, odontoplasty or tooth contouring, is a cosmetic dental procedure in which a dentist removes a small amount of the outer surface of a tooth to change its shape, length or edge. People use it to even out chipped, pointed or uneven teeth, balance the length of neighbouring teeth, soften overlapping edges and give the smile a more symmetrical, polished look.[1][2]

Descriptions of the procedure say it is quick, often completed in one visit of under an hour, and that enamel contains no nerve endings, so anaesthesia is frequently unnecessary.[3][2] The dentist reshapes the tooth with fine instruments such as burs, discs, strips or lasers and then polishes it; amounts on the order of 0.3 to 0.5 mm are cited for subtle changes.[3] It is often combined with bonding, whitening or other cosmetic work as part of smile design.[1][2]

Mature enamel has no cells or blood supply and is not renewed, so removal is permanent.[4] Sources stress conservative removal because enamel is thin, up to about 2.5 mm at the cusps.[4] The procedure suits minor irregularities; significant crowding or misalignment is addressed with orthodontics.[3][2]
infobox: Single visit, often under an hour[2]
Often not needed because enamel has no nerves[2]
Cosmetic dentistry is not recognised as a specialty by the American Dental Association[1]

paras: The procedure removes small amounts of enamel to correct chips, alter tooth length or shape, address differences in tooth size or smooth the look of slightly crooked teeth.[1] One source describes it as fast and says it can in some cases be used instead of braces for minor irregularities.[1] A further source reports amounts on the order of 0.3 to 0.5 mm for subtle changes, using diamond burs, discs, strips or lasers, followed by polishing.[3]
Consumer dental sources describe the steps as examination, reshaping or thinning of the enamel with specialised instruments, then smoothing and polishing, with immediate recovery.[2]

Enamel contouring is listed alongside whitening, bonding, veneers, bridges, implants and gum contouring as a standard cosmetic option.[1] It is often discussed as part of planned smile design, where tooth proportions and display are assessed together.[3] Veneers and crowns, by comparison, also require removing enamel, and enamel left unsupported by dentin is more prone to fracture.[4]

On looksmax.org, smile aesthetics come up in threads about gum show and lip lifts, where members ask about gum contouring in combination with lip surgery.[5] Enamel contouring itself is a smaller step than those procedures.

Sources agree that removed enamel cannot be replaced and that over-removal may expose dentin.[1][3] Temporary sensitivity to heat, cold or sweet foods is described as possible when enamel becomes thin.[3] Practitioners are described as favouring conservative, minimally invasive removal.[3] Enamel can be partly remineralised, for example with fluoride, but lost enamel cannot be restored by the body or a dentist.[4] Insurance often does not cover cosmetic reshaping.[2]

Cosmetic dentistry has been criticised in some quarters over informed consent, overtreatment and marketing, and the ADA does not approve the credentials of cosmetic-dentistry accreditation bodies.[1][3]

No studies found specific to enamel reshaping. Related dental research includes a comparison of digital and traditional crown extension guides in the aesthetic restoration of anterior teeth in 62 patients.[6]
